s: Lewis Mumford — The City in History
q: The 1961 book 'The City in History,' which called for basing technological power on society's fundamental needs and stressed a harmonious, ecologically balanced life for civilized social groups, was written by which urban theorist?
n: Lewis Mumford urged that fundamental needs of society be the bases for the judicious use of technological power — a power whose wonders obscure the better ends they might bring. These ends are the harmonious life of civilized social groups in ecological balance with the particular place occupied; he recognized the physical limitations of human settlements and wrote 'The City in History' (1961).

q: Which British planner (1879–1957), a pioneer of regional planning who led work on the Doncaster area and East Kent from 1920 to 1922 and later contributed to the Greater London Plan using open space as a structuring device, is being described?
n: Leslie Patrick Abercrombie (1879–1957) pioneered regional planning for the Doncaster area (1920–1922) and East Kent, and was involved in the Greater London Plan, using open space as a structuring element.

q: In 1767, which Scottish architect laid out linear new towns for Edinburgh, joining plazas, gridded houses, and open spaces on a plateau overlooking the city?
n: In 1767, Scottish architect James Craig planned linear new towns for Edinburgh, interconnected plazas, grid houses, and open spaces on a plateau overlooking the city.

q: Which figure, a forester by training who viewed the nation as divided along river drainage basins rather than state borders, authored 'An Open Space System for Appalachian America' and coined 'townless highway' and 'highwayless town'?
n: Benton Mackaye, originally a forester, saw the nation as a series of component parts whose natural divisions were river drainage areas, not state lines. He wrote 'An Open Space System for Appalachian America' and, in 'The New Exploration: A Philosophy of Regional Planning,' spoke of the 'townless highway' and the 'highwayless town' as mutually interdependent.

q: Working under his well-known pseudonym, which Swiss architect presented 'Une Ville Contemporaine' in 1922 as a hypothetical city for 3 million people, and later proposed the Radiant City to decongest urban centers by concentrating density on a small share of total ground area?
n: Swiss architect Charles Édouard Jeanneret (1887–1965), popularly known as Le Corbusier, unveiled 'Une Ville Contemporaine (Contemporary City)' in 1922, a hypothetical plan for a city of 3 million people exploiting technology; his ideas were traced to Eugene Henard's and Tony Garnier's work. He proposed 'La Ville Radieuse (Radiant City),' anchored on decongesting city centers by increasing density on a small part of the total ground area.

q: In 1799, which English social reformer built and ran an industrial village at New Lanark, framing it as a 'Village of Unity and Mutual Cooperation'?
n: In 1799, English social reformer Robert Owen constructed and operated an industrial village at New Lanark, a social and manufacturing community, conceptualizing the 'Village of Unity and Mutual Cooperation.'

q: Coined by Patrick Geddes in his 1915 book 'Cities in Evolution,' which term describes a conglomeration of town aggregates formed by waves of population inflow, overcrowding, backflow, and resulting sprawl?
n: In 'Cities in Evolution' (1915), Patrick Geddes coined the term 'conurbation,' meaning conglomeration of town aggregates, describing the waves of population inflow followed by overcrowding and slum formation, and the wave of backflow — the whole process resulting in amorphic sprawl, waste, and unnecessary obsolescence. Stages: Inflow → Build up → Backflow (center slums) → Sprawling mass (central blight).

q: Between 1879 and 1895, which chocolate manufacturer moved his factory to Bournville outside Birmingham, welcoming workers regardless of race or religion?
n: George Cadbury, a chocolate manufacturer, relocated his factory to Bournville outside of Birmingham (1879–1895), open to workers regardless of race or religion.

s: Frederick Law Olmsted — Conservationist & Park Movement
q: Often called the 'Father of Landscape Architecture' for his role in the American park movement, who designed New York's Central Park and Boston's 1880 Emerald Necklace Plan?
n: Frederick Law Olmsted, the 'Father of Landscape Architecture,' is associated with the American park system; he designed Central Park in New York and other parks in San Francisco, Buffalo, Detroit, and Montreal, as well as the Emerald Necklace Plan for Boston (1880). He believed cities should plan generations ahead to maintain sufficient breathing space, and in 1870 summed up his attitudes in 'Public Parks and the Enlargement of Towns.'

q: Complete the statement: the garden city of Letchworth, founded in 1902 some 35 miles from London, was planned by ___, both lieutenants of Ebenezer Howard.
n: Howard's lieutenants included Raymond Unwin and Barry Parker, who planned Letchworth, established in 1902, 35 miles from London, as the first garden city.

q: Which planning approach, suited to river-valley farming societies along the Nile, Tigris, and Euphrates, relied on the plow to lay out rectilinear plots for easy land division, crop planning, ownership records, and re-plotting after floods?
n: In the Ancient World, rectilinear plotting with the use of the plow suited the needs of agricultural societies on the Nile, Tigris, and Euphrates rivers for easy land division, land ownership, crop planning, and land plotting after a flood. It was used in ancient Greek towns, Roman colonial outposts, and Indian, Chinese, and pre-Columbian cities.

q: Who authored 'Man's Struggle for Shelter in an Urbanizing World' (1964), a work spanning highly developed to completely undeveloped nations that examined housing's central role in urban development and policy?
n: Charles Abrams saw housing as one of the prime fields of endeavor for solving urban problems; he wrote 'Man's Struggle for Shelter in an Urbanizing World' (1964), discussing the prime role of housing in urban development and rational policy, with his work and thought extending from highly developed to completely undeveloped nations.

q: During the City Beautiful Era (1900–1945), whose plan shaped the design of Canberra?
n: During the City Beautiful Era (1900–1945), Walter Burley Griffin (1875–1973) designed the plan for Canberra, Australia's capital.

s: Daniel Burnham — City Beautiful, criticized by Mumford
q: Daniel Burnham envisioned a City Beautiful–era city as a fully designed system of main circulation routes, parks, clusters, and focal civic buildings — but which critic dismissed this approach as merely cosmetic, likening it to totalitarian planning and faulting it for neglecting housing, schools, and sanitation?
n: Daniel Burnham's Plan of Chicago (1909) ushered in the golden age of urban design in the U.S., focused on monumental architecture and symbols of power. Lewis Mumford castigated Burnham's approach as cosmetic, comparing it to planning practiced in totalitarian regimes, arguing the plan ignored housing, schools, and sanitation, and devoted scant attention to zoning.

q: Which Japanese architect-planner, working on Tokyo, treated circulation as a key determinant of urban form and warned that once a city exceeds 2 to 3 million people, communication breaks down in a radiocentric layout shaped by unplanned growth?
n: Japanese architect-planner Kenzo Tange planned the city of Tokyo, emphasizing the role of circulation as a determinant of urban form, with a proposal based on penetrating analysis that cast light on problems, especially circulation. Accordingly, once a city grew beyond 2 or 3 million, vital communication becomes inefficient in a radiocentric city form created by spontaneous growth.

q: Whose 1962 book 'The Death and Life of Great American Cities' argued that high urban density was fine so long as buildings themselves weren't overcrowded, and urged leaving inner-city neighborhoods alone rather than letting planners rework them?
n: Jane Jacobs (1962) wrote 'The Death and Life of Great American Cities,' one of the most influential books in the history of city planning. She argued there was nothing wrong with high urban densities if they did not entail overcrowding in buildings, and prescribed keeping the inner-city neighborhood as it was before planners got their hands on it — that it should have more functions and land uses so people were there for different purposes and time schedules, using many facilities in common.

q: Between 1800 and 1810, which industrialist built an experimental industrial complex at New Lanark, Scotland, housing 1,000 workers with shared living, central heating, and private family lodgings?
n: Robert Owen built an experimental industrial settlement/complex at New Lanark, Scotland (1800–1810) — 1,000 strong communities having residence near the work place, communal living for old and children, central heating, and private lodging for families with children under 3, an agricultural village with some industry on the outskirts.

s: Town and Country Planning Act of 1947 — 'Hook'
q: Under Britain's Town and Country Planning Act of 1947, which 1950s scheme broke from prior practice by grouping houses tightly along a multi-level linear spine to shorten distances to communal facilities?
n: Under the Town and Country Planning Act of 1947 in Britain, a radical change in concept was introduced in the 1950s plan for 'Hook,' wherein houses were very closely grouped along a multi-level linear spine, decreasing distances so that all communal facilities could be reached by a short walk, with open countryside at the edge of the town.

q: Which scientist, in the 1950 book 'The Human Use of Human Beings,' introduced cybernetics — the study of control and communication in animals and machines — and helped shift planning away from fixed blueprints toward ongoing control of development?
n: Norbert Wiener wrote 'The Human Use of Human Beings' (1950), suggesting that automation would liberate the human race from the necessity of doing mundane tasks, and proposed a study of automatic control systems — cybernetics — the science of controls and communication in the animal and the machine. He was instrumental in changing the planning paradigm from producing blueprints for a desired future state toward a concept of planning as a continuous series of controls over development.

q: Hitler assigned which architect (1905–1981) the task of planning Berlin's reconstruction?
n: Albert Speer (1905–1981) was tasked by Hitler to plan the reconstruction of Berlin during the City Beautiful Era.

q: In 1910, which American envisioned a city where all vehicles traveled along the rooftops of one continuous building?
n: In 1910, American Edgar Chambless proposed a city with all vehicles running on the rooftops of a continuous building.

q: A 1600s plan for London proposed a network of avenues linking major landmarks, including St. Peter's and St. Paul's Cathedral — whose plan was this?
n: Sir Christopher Wren prepared a plan for London (i.e., St. Peter's and St. Paul's Cathedral), proposing a network of avenues connecting the main features of London.

q: Which American architect's designs for Central Philadelphia treated arterial stop-and-go streets and parking towers as central to urban form, arranging them into what he called a 'symphony of circulation'?
n: American architect Louis Kahn made important designs for Central Philadelphia, showing circulation — main arterial stop-and-go streets, and parking towers as key determinants of urban form, organized into a symphony of circulation.

q: Who founded the Council for the Preservation of Rural England?
n: Patrick Abercrombie was the founder of the Council for the Preservation of Rural England.

q: Which American architect-planner, author of 'The Disappearing City' and later 'Broadacres,' imagined every family settled on an acre of land and, in 1924, conceived Broadacre City as a rejection of big cities, finance capital, landlordism, and big government?
n: In the 1930s, American architect-planner Frank Lloyd Wright wrote 'The Disappearing City' and later 'Broadacres,' proposing that every family live on an acre of land, built by its inhabitants using mass-produced components. He conceived Broadacre City in 1924 as a symbol of his rejection of the big city (New York), finance capital, and landlordism, an anarchist rejection of government, believing in the liberating effects of new technologies and the homesteading principle.

s: Housing Act of 1949 and Jane Jacobs
q: The 1949 Housing Act, aimed at urban decay and requiring federal aid for buying blighted property under city redevelopment plans, set the stage for which urbanist's 1962 critique of urban renewal?
n: The Housing Act of 1949, which focused on urban decay, required federal aid to buy blighted property and cities to draw up redevelopment plans. This context set the stage for Jane Jacobs's 1962 book, 'The Death and Life of Great American Cities,' a landmark critique of urban renewal practices.

s: Clarence A. Perry — The Neighborhood Unit (1929)
q: In a 1929 book, which American architect-planner (1872–1944) proposed organizing towns into cohesive neighborhoods built around the natural service area of facilities like a primary school and shops?
n: Clarence A. Perry (1872–1944), an American architect-planner, discussed in his book 'The Neighborhood Unit' (1929) the idea of organizing towns into cohesive neighborhoods, applicable not only to new towns but to larger city areas; principles were based on the natural catchment area of community facilities such as primary schools and shops, and were copied by planners in Britain after his visit to the U.S.

q: By roughly what year had Rome, propelled by political power and organization, become the first city to reach a population of one million?
n: The Roman Empire was a vast city-building enterprise motivated by political power and organization; Rome became the first city with a million population by 3 A.D. Roman towns were basically military towns, with a system of gridiron streets enclosed by a wall, and public spaces such as theaters, arenas, and markets.

q: Ebenezer Howard's 'Tomorrow' (1902) — later retitled 'Garden Cities of Tomorrow' — launched the Garden City movement in Britain; what name is given to his framework showing that city and countryside each carry distinct pros and cons?
n: Ebenezer Howard wrote 'Tomorrow' (1902), followed by 'Garden Cities of Tomorrow.' His 'Three Magnets' paradigm depicted how the city and countryside had an indissoluble mixture of advantages and disadvantages — the city offered opportunities through jobs and urban services but resulted in a poor natural environment, while the countryside offered an excellent natural environment but virtually no opportunities.

q: In 1901, which French architect designed a hypothetical linear industrial town, 'Une Cité Industrielle,' notable for its emphasis on zoning and separation of functions, foreshadowing modern zoning practice?
n: In 1901, French architect Tony Garnier designed a hypothetical industrial town with a linear structure which he called 'Une Cité Industrielle.' This industrial town possessed a definite center but with a linear structure, with great emphasis on zoning and the separation of urban functions, anticipating modern zoning.

q: Which Italian futurist imagined an unsettling vision of a vast, motion-driven metropolis called 'La Città Nuova,' where every design element implied vertical or horizontal movement?
n: Italian futurist Antonio Sant'Elia provided a frightening vision of an enormous metropolis — 'La Città Nuova' — based on motion, with every element of its design implying vertical and horizontal circulation.

q: Whose 1066 conquest is linked to medieval towns growing around a monastery or castle, dependent on protective walls or fortifications for safety?
n: In Medieval Times, the growth of towns around either a monastery or a castle, relying on protective town walls or fortification for security, is associated with the Norman Empire under William the Conqueror; medieval towns generally were unplanned, organically evolving with an irregular street pattern, with abbeys and cathedrals indicating church influence and control.

q: Remembered for his 'ideal cities' — star-shaped layouts radiating streets from a central point typically anchored by a church, palace, or castle — which Renaissance architect-theorist is being described?
n: Leon Battista Alberti was the foremost early theoretician of the Renaissance, remembered for his 'ideal cities' — star-shaped plans with streets radiating from a central point, usually proposed for a church, palace, or castle, with curved streets conforming to topography.

q: Commissioned by Pope Sixtus V between 1585 and 1590 to draft a street plan for Rome's expansion, which architect marked key points across the city with tall obelisks as visual accents?
n: Domenico Pontana was commissioned by Pope Sixtus V to prepare and establish a street plan/framework for the growth of Rome, marking key points in the city with tall obelisks as visual accents of new streets.

q: In Ancient Greek town planning, what name is given to the central open space enclosed by surrounding buildings that served as its facades?
n: The Agora is a central open urban space in Ancient Greek town planning, where buildings served as facades to form an enclosed space, grouped around the central open area.

q: In 1811, which architect pursued an ambitious London scheme of grouping fine buildings around a park at the city's edge and linking it to the center via a grand avenue, realized through Regent Street, Regent Park, and Crescent?
n: In 1811, John Nash attempted an ambitious London concept, creating a fine group of buildings around a park at the city's edge, connecting the center of the city by a grand avenue, planning and carrying out work for Regent Street, Regent Park, and Crescent.

q: In Ancient Greek town planning, what term names the sacred hilltop precinct whose design reveals a clear relationship between buildings and the natural landscape?
n: In Hippodamus's Ancient Greek town planning, the Acropolis shows the visible relationship between buildings and nature, and is sacred.

q: Which French planner's 'The Cities of the Future' imagined buildings raised on stilts, traffic circles, and rooftops used for airplane landings?
n: French planner Eugene Henard published 'The Cities of the Future,' envisioning buildings on stilts, traffic circles, and airplane rooftop landings.

q: In 1899, which Russian geographer, author of 'Fields, Factories, Workshops,' argued electricity could let towns spring up anywhere and championed minimal government paired with maximum individual self-sufficiency?
n: In 1899, Russian geographer Peter Kropotkin published 'Fields, Factories, Workshops' — or 'Agriculture and Brainwork with Manual Work' — suggesting the use of electricity to allow towns to be built anywhere. He advocated minimal government at maximum individual self-sufficiency; his idea was to free town development with the use of electricity.

q: Napoleon III put whom in charge, starting in 1853, of rebuilding Paris (1850–1874) through history's largest public-works project, tearing down countless houses and turning the city into the 'City of Lights' that later inspired America's City Beautiful movement?
n: Baron Georges-Eugène Haussmann was made in charge by Napoleon III in 1853 to rebuild Paris (1850–1974); the rebuilding entailed the tearing down of many houses, was history's largest public works project, and Paris became the 'City of Lights,' a model for the American City Beautiful Era, later adopted by Daniel Burnham.

q: Whose plan for Brasília — the 20th century's largest planning undertaking, completed in four years by 600,000 workers — included no population projections, economic analysis, land-use schedule, model, or mechanical drawing, yet still won the commission?
n: Lucio Costa's plan or schemes for Brasília did not include a single population projection, economic analyses, land-use schedule, model, or mechanical drawing, yet it was awarded to him. Rio de Janeiro was bursting at the seams, so there was a need for a new capital in the interior; Brasília became the alternative site and the biggest planning exercise of the 20th century, finished within 4 years by 600,000 workers.

q: The early-1920s 'New Communities' Movement, whose members included Clarence Stein, Frederick Lee Ackerman, Lewis Mumford, Henry Churchill, Henry Wright, and Alexander Bing, produced the Radburn, New Jersey concept — what is the name of its design device, an island of green space ringed by homes and shielded by peripheral auto roads?
n: The New Communities' Movement felt that piecemeal development of residential communities on endless gridiron tracks was wasteful and prevented clustered community design. The Radburn, New Jersey idea created a series of superblocks — islands of greens bordered by homes and carefully skirted by peripheral auto roads — each around interconnected open green spaces, with greenways as pedestrian ways, aiming for the creation of neighborhood centers.

q: Which French-American engineer drew up the plan for Washington, D.C.?
n: Pierre Charles L'Enfant was a French American engineer who prepared the plan for Washington, D.C.

q: Who authored 'Inventory of World Resources — Human Trends and Needs' (1963), evaluating global productive capacity and proposing how it might be redirected entirely to humanity's benefit?
n: Buckminster Fuller wrote 'Inventory of World Resources — Human Trends and Needs' (1963), assessing the current state of the world's production and productive energy and suggesting how it can be turned to humanity's complete advantage.

q: In 1844, which planner proposed a 'Linear City' stretching from Cadiz, Spain, across Europe to St. Petersburg, Russia, arguing that linear utility infrastructure should govern all city layout?
n: In 1844, Don Arturo Soria y Mata proposed the 'Linear City' from Cadiz, Spain, across Europe through St. Petersburg, Russia, in which he proposed that the logic of linear utility lines should be the basis of all city layout, with houses and buildings set alongside linear utility systems supplying water, communications, and electricity, proposing high-speed, high-intensity transport from an existing city.

s: Eliel Saarinen — Modern Architecture and Planning
q: Which architect's award-winning Helsinki plan featured orderly community open space suited to island-and-bay topography, and who later wrote 'The City' (1943) advocating decentralizing large cities?
n: Eliel Saarinen proposed a prize-winning plan for Helsinki, with orderly and distinct community open space and an overall circulation pattern where elements suit the island and bay topography. In 1943, he wrote 'The City,' proposing the decentralization of large cities.

q: An early-19th-century architect-theorist whose main built work was Chaux, a salt-workers' town in France, championed loosely grouped housing arrangements centered on working-class needs in his 1804 book 'Architecture' — who was this?
n: Claude Nicolas Ledoux was an early-19th-century architect-theorist whose urban design attended to workers and the ruling class; his principal work was Chaux, a town for salt workers in France. He advocated informal grouping of houses and published 'Architecture' (1804), with theories striving toward the design of cities as a place to live with particular emphasis on the needs of the working class.

q: Which sociologist, disenchanted with top-down planning, cited the 1972 demolition of the Pruitt-Igoe housing project — 33 identical blocks totaling 2,800 apartments completed in 1955–56 and designed by Minoru Yamasaki — as emblematic of everything wrong with urban renewal?
n: Richard Sennett argued that in extricating the city from preplanned control, men will become more in control of themselves and each other. Disillusioned with the results of planning from above, he pointed to the demolition of the Pruitt-Igoe Housing Project — 33 identical blocks of 2,800 apartments completed in 1955–56, blown up 17 years later in 1972, designed by Japanese architect Minoru Yamasaki — as a symbol of all that was wrong with urban renewal.

s: Patrick Geddes — Birth of Regional Planning
q: Whose ideas, shaped by both French and Scottish influences, gave rise to the phrase 'Survey before Plan' and marked the beginning of regional planning around 1900?
n: Patrick Geddes (1854–1932) started the birth of regional planning; his ideas were derived from France and Scottish culture, and 'Survey before Plan' comes from Geddes. He asserted that the answer to the sordid congestion of the giant city is a vast program of regional planning within which each sub-regional part would be harmoniously developed based on its own natural resources.

q: Which Scottish-born planner, one of the founding figures of British Town Planning, directed the RPAA/RPA-produced eight-volume 1928 survey of the New York City Metropolitan Area?
n: Thomas Adams (1871–1940), one of the founding fathers of British Town Planning and first general manager of Letchworth Garden City, directed the Scottish-born-planner-led, 1928 eight-volume survey for the New York City Metropolitan Area, produced by the RPAA and the RPA (NY), which was criticized for its limits on physical scope.

s: Hippodamus of Miletus — Father of Town Planning
q: Credited as the 'Father of Town Planning' and active around 500–400 B.C., which Greek architect designed Priene and Piraeus and is associated with the gridiron street pattern?
n: Hippodamus of Miletus (500–400 B.C.) was a Greek architect who planned Priene and Piraeus, emphasizing geometric designs and the grid pattern of streets. He is credited with the gridiron pattern, and is remembered for the Acropolis (relationship between buildings and nature) and the Agora (buildings as facades enclosing an urban space).

q: In 1888, which chemical-industry magnate relocated his soap factory to Port Sunlight on the Mersey, building a village of employee cottages each with a small back garden?
n: William Lever, a chemical magnate, relocated his factory to Port Sunlight on the Mersey (1888) — more of a village for his soap factory employees, with cottages having small back gardens.

q: Which Vienna-born figure, involved in the 'Rebuilding Berkeley' project, held that residents must be directly engaged in construction for a place to feel alive and beautiful, and championed subsidized self-directed neighborhood change?
n: Viennese-born Christopher Alexander developed the idea that groups of people might change their own environment, subsidized from above; in the project 'Rebuilding Berkeley,' 'People' developed the idea of self-sustaining, self-governing neighborhoods (though it didn't work). He believed that for things to become alive and beautiful, it is necessary for people to be directly involved in the act of construction rather than fiddling.

q: Whose 10-volume treatise 'De Arkitektura' merged architecture and town design into a single subject, establishing the groundwork for theoretical design thinking, as a Roman architect?
n: Vitruvius was a Roman architect whose 10-volume treatise 'De Arkitektura' relates the experience of Roman architecture and town design, suggesting the location of streets in relation to prevailing wind, the siting of public buildings, the testing of drinking water, and the design of plazas.

q: In 1829, which French social reformer's 'The New World of Industry and Society' proposed housing 400 families in a single palace-like structure called the 'Phalanstery'?
n: In 1829, French social reformer Francois Fourier published 'The New World of Industry and Society,' envisioning putting 400 families into a palace-like building he called the 'Phalanstery.'

q: In his 'Codex Atlanticus,' which Renaissance polymath sketched a Milan redesign in which a river's upstream portion split into 6 or 7 parallel branches before rejoining downstream, meant to remedy the ills of squalor and overcrowding?
n: In his 'Codex Atlanticus,' Leonardo da Vinci, thinking as a town planner, described a new urban planning concept suited for Milan — sketching a city straddling a river with the upstream divided into 6 or 7 branches, parallel to the main stream, rejoining it below the city — as a cure for urban disease caused by squalor and unhealthful crowding.

q: Which British-born architect designed the striking Byker Wall housing redevelopment, built through ongoing dialogue with its future residents?
n: British-born architect Ralph Erskine built the remarkable Byker Wall, a redevelopment housing project designed for continuous dialogue with the residents.

q: Coining the term 'Ekistics' — the science of human settlements — and authoring 'Architecture in Transition' (1963) plus the 'Ekistic Grids' system, which urban theorist tackled worldwide urbanization?
n: Constantine Doxiadis addressed problems of urbanization worldwide, publishing his 'Ekistic Grids,' a system for recording planning data, and wrote 'Architecture in Transition' (1963). He approached town planning as a science incorporating contributions from sociologists, geographers, economists, demographers, and others, assembling them into a total rational and human approach he called 'Ekistics' — the science of human settlements.

s: The Regional Planning Association of America (RPAA)
q: Formed in 1923 from the alliance of Mumford, Stein, Chase, MacKaye, Whiteaker, Ackerman, Wright, and Bing, which organization published 'Survey,' a manifesto centered on the concept of the region?
o: The Regional Planning Association of America (RPAA)
The Council for the Preservation of Rural England
n: The Regional Planning Association of America (RPAA), founded in 1923, arose from the close association of Mumford, Stein, Chase, MacKaye, Whiteaker, Ackerman, Wright, and Bing. It published 'Survey' — a manifesto constituting one of the most important documents of history, devoted to the concept of the region.

q: Nicknamed the 'Master Builder,' who oversaw execution of the New York Plan?
n: Robert Moses, known as the 'Master Builder,' was in charge of the implementation of the New York Plan.

q: Between 1853 and 1863, which industrialist established a wooden mill town around his textile operation in Saltaire, near Bradford, England?
n: Titus Salt built a wooden mill town around his textile mill in Saltaire near Bradford, England (1853–1863) — a model industrial community, though with an uninspired, monotonous grinding pattern, with easy access to open country.

s: Henry Wright — Regional Planning for New York
q: Working under a commission chaired by Clarence Stein, who produced the 'Report of the Commission on Housing and Regional Planning for the State of New York,' proposing that clusters of smaller communities like Radburn, New Jersey, could absorb urban growth?
n: Working under a commission chaired by Stein, Henry Wright produced the 'Report of the Commission on Housing and Regional Planning for the State of New York,' explaining how New York developed from small trade centers into a financial and managerial center, and proposing that a core of constellations of smaller communities like Radburn, New Jersey, could accommodate growth.

q: Who demonstrated that livable, workable towns could arise within a capitalist system through the 'Social City' model of decentralized jobs, multiple settlement centers, garden cities, and suburban growth?
n: Ebenezer Howard showed how workable and livable towns could be formed within a capitalist framework through the 'Social City' concept, whereby decentralized employment, polycentric settlements, garden cities, and suburban expansion combine. In 1902, a garden city was established at Letchworth, 35 miles from London, planned by Barry Parker and Raymond Unwin.

q: Regarded as one of the Western world's earliest modern urban designers, who restored and mapped out the future growth of Ferrara, a city considered thoroughly modern by 1860?
n: Biaggio Rosetti is regarded as one of the western world's earliest modern urban designers; he repaired an existing city and planned for its future expansion in Ferrara, considered a modern city in Europe by 1860.

q: Known as both the 'Father of American City Planning' and the 'Prophet of the City Beautiful Movement in America,' who authored the 1909 Plan for Chicago, drawing on Haussmann's Paris and Vienna reconstructions?
n: Daniel Burnham, American 'Father of American City Planning' and 'Prophet of the City Beautiful Movement in America,' wrote 'Plan for Chicago' (1909) and 'Planning the Region of Chicago' (1956); its origins were based on the boulevards and promenades of great European capitals, including Haussmann's reconstruction of Paris and Vienna. His greatest achievement was the Chicago Plan of 1909.

q: Whose 1766 plan, 'London and Westminster Improved,' is credited with ushering in a Golden Age of building in London?
n: In 1766, John Gwynn produced the remarkable plan 'London and Westminster Improved,' addressing London's growth and re-development; the plan heralded a Golden Age of building in London.

q: Which U.S. railroad engineer and inventor of the Pullman railway car built a model industrial town on 4,000 acres of wetland outside Chicago starting in 1880?
n: George Pullman, a U.S. railroad engineer and inventor of Pullman cars, built the model industrial town of Pullman outside of Chicago, Illinois (1880 onwards), on 4,000 acres of wetland.
